issues.legal_issue: A purported partition deed made to defeat family members’ rights and not acted upon is a sham transaction.
material_facts: The two brothers divided the lands unequally, while the deed made no provision for division of the family house.
The brothers continued in joint possession of the lands, lived in the same house, and maintained a joint mess after the deed.
The circumstances supported the finding that the deed was intended to limit the widows’ claims to the smaller share and avoid consequences of a possible adoption.
Both lower courts found the deed was not genuine.
issues.conclusion: The partition deed was sham and was not intended to be effective.
issues.legal_principle: The Court ordinarily accepts concurrent findings of fact in an appeal by special leave unless they lack evidentiary support. The evidence supported the finding that the deed was a sham, including the unequal division and the family’s continued joint living and possession. The uncertainty before Anant v. Shankar, A.I.R. 1943 P.C. 196, concerning the effect of a widow’s adoption on family property also supported the inference that the deed was intended to avoid possible legal consequences.

rule.if: special_leave_appeal_challenges_concurrent_finding and partition_deed_dispute and unequal_division and continued_joint_living and continued_joint_possession and deed_intended_to_defeat_family_claims

predicates.special_leave_appeal_challenges_concurre: The proceeding is an appeal by special leave challenging a factual finding reached by both lower courts.
predicates.partition_deed_dispute: The dispute concerns whether a document purporting to divide family property was a genuine partition.
predicates.unequal_division: The purported partition allocated substantially unequal shares of the family lands.
predicates.continued_joint_living: The family members continued living together in the same home after the document was made.
predicates.continued_joint_possession: The family members continued possessing the lands jointly after the document was made.
predicates.deed_intended_to_defeat_family_claims: The circumstances showed that the document was intended to defeat or restrict the claims of other family members.

issues.definition: When a special leave appeal challenges concurrent findings in a partition dispute, and the unequal division, continued joint living and possession, and purpose of defeating family claims support those findings, the document is treated as a sham.

issues.legal_issue: A sham expression of an intention to partition does not sever joint family status.
material_facts: The brothers relied on the purported partition deed as an expression of an intention to separate.
The deed was found to be a sham and was not intended to be effective.
The brothers continued in joint possession and continued living together after the deed.
issues.conclusion: The sham deed did not sever the joint family status.
issues.legal_principle: A definite and unequivocal indication by one coparcener of an intention to separate can sever joint status without the assent of the others, once clearly communicated. But an expression of intention that is merely a pretence or sham has no such effect. The Court applied Merla Ramanna v. Chelikani Jagannadha Rao, A.I.R. 1941 P.C. 48.

predicates.joint_family_status_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether members of a family remained joint in status.
predicates.purported_separation_expression: A family member relied on an expressed intention or document as showing an intention to separate.
predicates.expression_was_sham: The expression or document was not genuine and was merely a pretence.

issues.definition: In a dispute over joint family status, a purported separation expression that was merely a sham does not result in severance.

issues.legal_issue: Later acquisitions are presumed to be joint family property when an adequate family-property nucleus could have funded them and no separate source of funds is established.
material_facts: The family possessed ancestral lands that the lower courts found constituted an adequate nucleus for the later purchases.
The income from the nucleus was more than sufficient to acquire the later lands.
The later acquisitions were made over a period of years, and the claimed separate business income of the acquiring family member was not proved.
issues.conclusion: The later-acquired lands were joint family properties.
issues.legal_principle: Joint family status alone creates no presumption that a family possesses joint property or that a member’s acquisition is joint. The person claiming an item as joint family property initially bears the burden of proof. Once an adequate nucleus capable of funding the acquisition is established, the burden shifts to the person claiming self-acquisition to prove that the property was acquired without aid from the family estate. The Court applied Appalaswami v. Suryanarayanamurti, I.L.R. [1948] Mad. 440 (P.C.), and referred to Babubhai Girdharlal v. Ujamlal Hargovandas, Venkataramayya v. Seshamma, and Vythianatha v. Varadaraja.

rule.if: partition_property_dispute and adequate_family_nucleus and nucleus_could_fund_acquisition and separate_source_not_proved

predicates.partition_property_dispute: The proceeding concerns the division of property claimed to belong to a joint family.
predicates.adequate_family_nucleus: The family possessed joint property that formed an adequate nucleus.
predicates.nucleus_could_fund_acquisition: The income or value of the nucleus was sufficient to fund the disputed acquisition.
predicates.separate_source_not_proved: The person claiming the acquisition as separate property did not prove an independent source of funds.

issues.definition: In a partition-property dispute, a later acquisition is treated as joint family property when an adequate family nucleus could have funded it and no separate source is proved.

issues.legal_issue: A sale may be held not binding on a claimant when the claimant challenged the alienations in the pleadings and the sale was unsupported by consideration.
material_facts: The plaint challenged the alienations generally, sought relief concerning the scheduled lands, and included the lands covered by the sale.
The purchaser was a minor, the seller acted as her guardian, and the purchaser had no property of her own.
The High Court found the sale to be without consideration and not genuine.
issues.conclusion: The sale was not binding on the claimant.
issues.legal_principle: A pleading that challenges alienations generally and seeks relief concerning the scheduled properties can encompass a sale even if the sale is not specifically identified in the paragraph relied on by the opposing party, where the relevant properties are included in the schedule. The Court upheld the finding that this sale was without consideration and not genuine.

rule.if: partition_suit_with_cross_objection and plaint_challenges_alienations and disputed_property_in_schedule and sale_without_consideration

predicates.partition_suit_with_cross_objection: The proceeding is a partition suit in which a cross-objection challenges the treatment of a property sale.
predicates.plaint_challenges_alienations: The claimant’s pleadings challenge the family’s alienations and seek relief concerning them.
predicates.disputed_property_in_schedule: The property covered by the sale is included in the property schedule to the pleadings.
predicates.sale_without_consideration: The sale was found to be unsupported by consideration and not genuine.

issues.definition: In a partition suit with a cross-objection, a scheduled property sale challenged by the pleadings and found to be without consideration is not binding on the claimant.
